facts.statement: Chenanisaurus was described in 2017 by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues.
facts.quote: Chenanisaurus was described in 2017 by British paleontologist Nicholas Longrich and colleagues.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Morocco.
facts.quote: Chenanisaurus (meaning "Sidi Chennane lizard") is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Morocco.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus belongs to the family Abelisauridae.
facts.quote: The genus belongs to the family Abelisauridae.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus is one of the few known African members of the family Abelisauridae.
facts.quote: Chenanisaurus is one of few known African members of Abelisauridae.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus was estimated to be 7 to 8 meters long, making it one of the largest known abelisaurids.
facts.quote: Its length is estimated to be around 7 - 8 m, making it among the largest known abelisaurids.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus existed approximately one million years before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
facts.quote: Chenanisaurus was among the last non-avian dinosaurs, existing just one million years prior to the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus lived in the Ouled Abdoun Basin, which was a marine environment at the time.
facts.quote: It was found in the Ouled Abdoun Basin, which was a marine environment at the time Chenanisaurus lived.

facts.statement: Fossils of Chenanisaurus were first discovered in the Sidi Chennane mines near Khouribga in northern Morocco.
facts.quote: Fossils of Chenanisaurus were first discovered in the phosphate mine of Couche III, an outcrop of the Ouled Abdoun Basin in the Sidi Chennane mines outside of Khouribga in northern Morocco.

facts.statement: Additional fossils assigned to Chenanisaurus include two premaxillary teeth and a maxillary tooth found at Sidi Daoui or Sidi Chennane.
facts.quote: Additionally, two premaxillary teeth from Sidi Daoui and a maxillary tooth found at either Sidi Chennane or Sidi Daoui also belong to Chenanisaurus.

facts.statement: The fossils of Chenanisaurus date to the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: The Ouled Abdoun Basin, where these fossils were found, date to the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The name Chenanisaurus combines the location Sidi Chennane with the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: The generic name Chenanisaurus is derived from Sidi Chennane, where the dentary was found, and the Greek root "sauros" meaning "lizard".

facts.statement: The species name barbaricus refers to the Greek word for barbaric and the Barbary Coast of Morocco.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from the Greek word "barbaros" meaning "barbaric" and also refers to Barbary, as in the Barbary Coast of Morocco and northwest Africa.

facts.statement: The incomplete dentary serves as the holotype specimen for Chenanisaurus.
facts.quote: The incomplete dentary was chosen as the holotype (name-bearing) specimen, whereas the premaxillary teeth and maxillary tooth were assigned based on size, traits, and provenance.

facts.statement: A maxillary tooth assigned to Chenanisaurus was originally described in 2005 as belonging to an indeterminate abelisaurid.
facts.quote: The maxillary tooth assigned to Chenanisaurus had previously been described in a 2005 study by French paleontologist Eric Buffetaut and colleagues, which stated the tooth came from an indeterminate abelisaurid theropod.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus was a bipedal carnivore.
facts.quote: Being an abelisaurid theropod, Chenanisaurus would have been a bipedal (two-legged) carnivore.

facts.statement: The holotype dentary of Chenanisaurus is missing its posterior end and is damaged in several areas.
facts.quote: The dentary is missing its posterior (back) end and is damaged in several areas.

facts.statement: The dentary preserves ten tooth positions, including three preserved crowns and four broken crowns.
facts.quote: It preserves ten alveoli (tooth positions) with three preserved tooth crowns and four broken crowns.

facts.statement: The first tooth of Chenanisaurus was small, a trait shared with other ceratosaurs.
facts.quote: The first tooth was small, a trait observed in other ceratosaurs (the group containing abelisaurids and noasaurids).

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus had a proportionately short and tall lower jaw.
facts.quote: Relative to the dimensions of the alveoli, the dentary is deep, implying Chenanisaurus had a proportionately short, tall lower jaw.

facts.statement: The dentary of Chenanisaurus was bowed ventrally, similar to Carnotaurus.
facts.quote: The dorsal and ventral (top and bottom) margins of the dentary are curved in lateral (side) view, indicating that the bone was bowed ventrally like in Carnotaurus.

facts.statement: The front margin of Chenanisaurus's dentary is almost vertical, unlike the rounded margins of Majungasaurus and Ekrixinatosaurus.
facts.quote: The front margin of the dentary is almost vertical, in contrast to the rounded front margins of Majungasaurus and Ekrixinatosaurus.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus has deep interdental plates ornamented with shallow grooves.
facts.quote: Chenanisaurus interdental plates are deep, a feature of derived abelisaurids, and are ornamented with shallow grooves.

facts.statement: The mandible of Chenanisaurus was U-shaped and broad when viewed from above.
facts.quote: The curvature of the dentary suggests that the mandible was U-shaped and broad in dorsal (top) view.

facts.statement: A groove runs along the length of the lateral surface of Chenanisaurus's dentary.
facts.quote: The lateral (outside) surface of the dentary bears a groove that runs along its length.

facts.statement: The groove on the dentary is bordered by foramina that open into dorsally-extended sulci.
facts.quote: This groove is bordered dorsally by a pattern of foramina (small openings) that open upwards into dorsally-extended sulci (grooves).

facts.statement: The pattern of grooves and foramina on Chenanisaurus's dentary differs from derived taxa like Carnotaurus, where the groove is lower.
facts.quote: This pattern of grooves and foramina is found in other abelisaurids, but in derived taxa like Carnotaurus the groove is situated lower on the dentary.

facts.statement: The dentary condition of Chenanisaurus is more similar to the basal ceratosaur Genyodectes than to other abelisaurids.
facts.quote: The condition in Chenanisaurus is more similar to that of the basal ceratosaur Genyodectes than other abelisaurids, showing its distinctness from other abelisaurids.

facts.statement: The alveoli of Chenanisaurus are rectangular when viewed from above.
facts.quote: The alveoli are rectangular in dorsal (top) view.

facts.statement: The dentary of Chenanisaurus carries at least ten teeth.
facts.quote: The dentary carries at least ten teeth, though there are fifteen dentary teeth in other abelisaurids like Carnotaurus.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus teeth change shape posteriorly, with front teeth having a D-shaped cross-section and rear teeth being flatter and dagger-shaped.
facts.quote: The teeth change in shape going posteriorly, with the front teeth having a D-shaped cross section and a convex anterior face whereas the rear teeth are flatter and dagger-shaped.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Chenanisaurus teeth show up to thirteen denticles per 5 mm at the base and up to eight near the apex.
facts.quote: The cutting edges are convex and show up to thirteen denticles (serrations) per 5 mm at the crown base and up to eight denticles near the apex.

facts.statement: The maxillary tooth of Chenanisaurus has a total height of 58 mm and a crown height of 37 mm.
facts.quote: As for the maxillary tooth specifically, its total height is 58 mm, with a crown height of 37 mm.

facts.statement: The enamel of Chenanisaurus teeth is smooth except for a weak wrinkle near the base of the crown.
facts.quote: The enamel is smooth, except for a weak wrinkle located towards the base of the crown.

facts.statement: It is debated whether enamel wrinkles on Chenanisaurus teeth are unique features or caused by growth anomalies.
facts.quote: Enamel wrinkles have been found on other theropods besides Carcharodontosaurus and Chenanisaurus, but they typically are due to growth anomalies in tooth formation.

facts.statement: A 2020 analysis by Delcourt and Iori recovered Chenanisaurus as the sister taxon of the unnamed Pourcieux taxon.
facts.quote: In their phylogenetic analysis, Delcourt and Iori (2020) recovered Chenanisaurus as the sister taxon of an unnamed abelisaurid known as the Pourcieux taxon.

facts.statement: Chenanisaurus lived during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous, about one million years before the Chicxulub asteroid impact.
facts.quote: These dinosaurs would have lived in the very latest Cretaceous (late Maastrichtian), approximately 1 million years before the Chicxulub asteroid impact that caused the KPg Extinction Event.

facts.statement: All known fossils of Chenanisaurus come from the phosphate deposits of the Ouled Abdoun Basin in north-central Morocco.
facts.quote: All known specimens of Chenanisaurus have been recovered from the phosphates of the Ouled Abdoun Basin of north-central Morocco.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Morocco may have functioned as an isolated island during the time Chenanisaurus lived.
facts.quote: Morocco itself may have been an isolated island.

facts.statement: The marine location of Chenanisaurus fossils suggests the theropod dragged itself into the sea after death, where the holotype fossilized.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Chenanisaurus represents a distinct lineage of abelisaurids separate from South American, Indian-Madagascan, and European forms, supporting the hypothesis that Gondwana's fragmentation led to endemic dinosaur faunas.
